newsitem.title: UK: SOCCER-ENGLAND AGAIN LOSE OUT TO QUALITY OPPONENTS.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-ENGLAND AGAIN LOSE OUT TO QUALITY OPPONENTS.

text.p: England reflected on Thursday on another valiant Wembley performance against world class opposition and another heart-breaking defeat.
"It just didn't happen for us," striker Alan Shearer acknowledged. "We had one or two half chances but it was not enough."
Veteran defender Stuart Pearce accepted England had paid the price for a momentary lapse in defence despite dominating possession in their 1-0 World Cup qualifying defeat by Italy.
"When you are in the top six sides in the world, that's what separates you," he said. "The ball came over the top and (Gianfranco) Zola nipped in behind. His first touch was extremely good."
Glenn Hoddle's side had thrown everything at Italy on Wednesday night, but in the end the superbly-marshalled visiting defence won through.
Their extra touch of class showed on the handful of occasions they turned defence into counter-attack and the English created nothing as threatening as Zola's crisp 19th minute winner.
It was England's biggest match since last year's European championship semifinal against Germany in the same stadium.
Then too, England had the lion's share of the ball and were equals with the Germans for 120 pulsating minutes of open play.
When it came to a penalty shoot-out though, Germany, like Italy on Wednesday, showed they are still have an edge on the English in terms of experience, composure and tactical acumen.
Southampton's mercurial forward Matt Le Tissier was the obvious scapegoat for the English media.
His inclusion was Hoddle's big gamble and it was Le Tissier who missed England's best chance, heading wide in the first half with Italian goalkeeper Angelo Peruzzi flapping at thin air.

"Perhaps Glenn Hoddle should have given up gambling for Lent," the Independent newspaper reflected on Thursday. "He risked England's hopes on the sloping shoulders of Matt Le Tissier. The gamble failed."
But in truth, Le Tissier's 60th minute replacement by Newcastle striker Les Ferdinand made little real difference to England's onslaught on the thicket of blue shirts guarding Peruzzi's goal.

The Italian defence, under strict orders from new coach Cesare Maldini and governed by sweeper Alessandro Costacurta seemed capable of subduing just about anyone on a blustery, rainy evening which made the euphoria and the balmy summer evenings of Euro 96 seem like ancient history.
"Almost every time Italy touched the ball there was evidence of the disparity in quality," the Times said. "The premier league the best in the world? You must be joking."
Match statistics showed that England had 61 percent of the ball to Italy's 39. They had 18 attempts on goal to Italy's seven. England were on target eight times, the Italians twice.

But those figures embarrass the English rather than excuse them, and Hoddle must now be worried about his side's ability to break down the world's toughest defences -- even with Alan Shearer in his forward line.

They face a tricky World Cup qualifier in Poland before travelling to Italy in November for their final group two match -- a game they may need to win to stand a chance of qualification for France 1998.
Wednesday's defeat also brought to an end a pround English record in World Cup matches -- it was their first home defeat in soccer's premier event.
